topStories.headline: Burgum Tells Presidio Residents: No Sell-Off, But Rent Fears Remain
topStories.dek: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum attended Wednesday's Presidio Trust board meeting in person, pledging no land sales — but tenants pressed the new Trump-appointed board over escalating rents.
topStories.body:
U.S. Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum appeared at the Presidio Trust's public board of directors meeting on the evening of November 12 at the Presidio Officers' Club, the first in-person meeting of the board since President Trump fired its previous six members and installed replacements earlier this year. Burgum spoke after a closed session and pushed back against mounting public concern that the administration intends to sell or develop portions of the historic former Army base. "There will be no sell-off; we're not selling an acre of The Presidio," Burgum said, according to KTVU.

But the secretary's assurances did not fully quiet the crowd. Tenants who live in the Presidio's roughly 1,400 residential units — home to about 3,100 people — raised the issue of rapidly rising rents. The Presidio's housing is exempt from San Francisco's rent-control law and other city tenant protections, and earlier reporting by the San Francisco Chronicle found that some residents had received increases averaging about 5.5 percent, with some as high as 10 percent, as the Trust adjusted rents to market levels while seeking revenue to address a $500 million deferred maintenance backlog.

Supervisor Stephen Sherrill, whose District 2 encompasses the Presidio, had previously told the Chronicle he was pushing for a formal meeting between residents and Trust leadership. That request appears to have made some headway: a follow-up meeting between the Trust and the neighborhood association is now being scheduled for December, according to KTVU. The board's agenda on Wednesday included a fiscal year 2026 review and a preview of fiscal year 2027 priorities, as well as updates from the National Park Service and the Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy.

topStories.headline: SF's First Lego Resale Shop Is Coming to Clement Street
topStories.dek: A family-run business called The Missing Brick plans to open at 843 Clement Street in spring 2027, filling a gap left when the city's only official Lego store closed in 2023.
topStories.body:
The Inner Richmond is set to get a one-of-a-kind addition to its retail mix: The Missing Brick, San Francisco's first dedicated Lego resale store, plans to open in spring 2027 at 843 Clement Street, the address previously occupied by Apple Land Produce, SFist reported on November 12.

The shop will buy, sell, and trade new and used Lego sets, Minifigures, and individual pieces — a niche that has gone unserved since the city's only official Lego store, at San Francisco Centre downtown, permanently closed in 2023. The owners, described as longtime Inner Richmond residents, have been testing the concept through pop-up events around the city before committing to a permanent storefront. The store will also host events aimed at both younger builders and adult collectors. No opening date beyond "spring 2027" has been announced.

topStories.headline: Richmond Residents Grade City Services — and Push for Results
topStories.dek: About 60 neighbors gathered in October at the Richmond Recreation Center to give city agency representatives a candid assessment of what is working and what is not in District 1.
topStories.body:
Roughly 60 Richmond District residents convened at the Richmond Recreation Center on October 22 for a neighborhood budget summit organized by outgoing District 1 Supervisor Connie Chan. Chan, who is leaving the Board of Supervisors after losing her congressional primary to Scott Wiener, described the summit series as a way to verify that the city's nearly $17 billion annual budget is actually funding what residents need. The Richmond Review reported on the gathering on November 10.

Attendees told city agency representatives what the district does well and where service gaps remain. The Board of Supervisors is expected to use the feedback as an input into the next city budget cycle, and the city is posting summaries of each summit online in the weeks after each event. One participant, identified as Li, raised the broader question of translation: "I think at this point the real question is how is the City going to take in all the feedback coming from all these different family summits and turn that into something actionable," they said, according to the Richmond Review.

The format was adapted from a similar process used in District 7 and proposed for District 1. With Chan departing after her congressional concession last week, the question of who will carry the effort forward — and who will represent the Richmond on the Board — remains open.

moreNews.headline: Geary Boulevard Underground Work Done; Street-Level Construction Up Next
moreNews.body: The SFPUC confirmed as of October 9 that its Geary Boulevard Sewer and Water Improvements Phase 2 project is 100 percent complete, finishing ahead of its original schedule. The work, which began in January 2025, replaced aging sewer and water pipes along Geary from Stanyan Street to 32nd Avenue — infrastructure that in some places dated to the late 1800s. With the underground contractor demobilized, attention now shifts above ground: the SFMTA is set to begin transit and pedestrian-safety improvements along the same corridor this fall, with full repaving expected to follow. That surface work is projected to run through early 2028.

moreNews.headline: SFUSD Ends Lottery; Richmond Families to Get Neighborhood School Guarantees
moreNews.body: The San Francisco Unified School District board voted 5-2 on October 13 to replace its 15-year-old school-assignment lottery with a neighborhood-based system. Under the approved plan, known as Option C, elementary students will be assigned to a school based on their home address, with continued access to citywide special programs including language immersion and bilingual education. Supporters of the Richmond and Sunset neighborhoods have long favored neighborhood placement; the Richmond Review noted on November 10 that families guaranteed a local spot may be less likely to leave the public system. The new policy takes effect for the 2028-29 school year, with SFUSD staff tasked with drawing updated attendance boundaries and presenting a full implementation plan to the board in April 2027.

moreNews.headline: SFPD Arrests Woman at 32nd Avenue Home on Multiple Charges
moreNews.body: San Francisco police arrested a 42-year-old woman on November 6 while executing a search warrant at a residence on the 200 block of 32nd Avenue in the Richmond District. Officers booked Diana Peng at San Francisco County Jail on charges including fraud, being a felon in possession of a firearm and ammunition, narcotics offenses, driving without a license, and improper care of animals. The SFPD described the investigation as ongoing and open. Anyone with information is asked to contact the department at 415-575-4444.
